Hot Stocks

Before deciding to move out of his parents’ home last year, Kevin Martin carefully crafted a budget that would allow him to get an apartment with three roommates in nearby Tempe, Arizona, while he attended Mesa Community College. The accounting major made it work by holding down three part-time jobs and was even able to save as much as $200 a month.

But Martin, 19, couldn’t predict that Arizona would have an unusually warm spring that led to a big jump in monthly air conditioning costs.

The foursome tried to keep the electricity bills in check by turning off the AC when they were out, but they’d return to a home that felt like a sauna. He knew it would only get worse during the summer

So Martin decided to move back home, his goal of living independently derailed by higher bills, from air conditioning to gas to groceries amid the ongoing US war with Iran.

“Over the months, I was saving less money and spending more,” said Martin, who realized it was “probably smarter to go back home so I could save more money … I didn’t really want to spend all that money on AC.”

Martin got an early taste of what many Americans will likely experience this summer – a steep increase in the cost of keeping cool.

Electricity bills are expected to jump an average of 10.5%, to $792, nationwide for June through September, according to the latest National Energy Assistance Directors Association projection. The outlook takes into account both higher electricity prices and greater air conditioning usage amid forecasts for above-average temperatures for much of the nation.

The increase adds to the financial squeeze that many Americans are feeling as annual inflation in May topped 4% for the first time in three years, pushed up by the surge in fuel and other costs in the wake of the Iran war. As of April, wages are no longer exceeding inflation.

Staying cool during the summer has been growing ever more expensive in recent years – up nearly 40% since 2020, according to the association.

Some states are seeing more folks with higher incomes apply for assistance with their utility bills, said Mark Wolfe, the association’s executive director.

“Middle- and moderate-income families are struggling to pay basic expenses,” he said.

The US Department of Energy offers a variety of tips for keeping spring and summer energy bills in check as temperatures warm. They include: installing window coverings; setting thermostats higher, especially when not at home; maintaining cooling equipment and vacuuming air intake vents; and sealing cracks and air leaks around windows and doors.

Alisha Hamid, who works in sales, thinks that she makes a decent income but still finds it hard to stay on top of her ever-rising expenses. She is shelling out close to $600 a month for electricity at her Egg Harbor Township, New Jersey, home, nearly the cost of her mortgage and double what she was paying only a few years ago. It might have been manageable if the prices for other necessities, such as gas and groceries, remained flat, she said.

Hamid, 34, is having a tough time explaining to her 8-year-old daughter, Angelina, why they can no longer afford to go to a water park that they like about an hour away. Instead, the single mom plans to get a season pass to a local, less expensive, water park.

“Every time I feel I’m getting ahead, prices go up and the finish line gets farther away,” said Hamid, who is waiting to hear whether she qualifies for the federal Low Income Home Energy Assistance Program, known as LIHEAP.

Christina Meikrantz had also hoped to get help from LIHEAP.

But the software support technician, who is raising two children on her own, was told she makes too much money – even though she considers herself among the “working poor.”

The Benton, Pennsylvania, resident paid about $190 for electricity in May, up 41% from the same month last year. She’s trying to minimize air conditioner usage by turning on only one unit in the house at a time, using fans and putting up blackout curtains in the dining and living rooms. She plans to set up kiddie pools outside to help keep her three dogs cool.

Meikrantz, 46, is also considering getting a second job, though she really doesn’t want to work 60-hour weeks. But she feels overwhelmed by all her expenses and is worried about having her electricity disconnected if she falls behind.

“I’m afraid to get my next bill,” she said. “Inflation is going up, but unfortunately, paychecks are not.”

What is driving prices higher for summer getaways?

More than 13 million disconnections occurred in 2024, far more than some experts thought, according to a recent report from the Energy Information Administration.

While most states protect their residents from having their heat shut off in the winter, the same can’t be said for electricity in the summer.

Only 19 states and the District of Columbia have summer shutoff protections, and they are typically less comprehensive than winter protections. The summer provisions are typically triggered when temperatures reach a certain level or when heat emergencies are declared, instead of the blanket winter disconnection moratoriums.

The consequences of extreme heat aren’t taken as seriously as extreme cold, even as summer heat waves become more frequent and intense as the climate changes, experts said. Summer protections, as weak as they are, should take into account humidity, not only temperatures, they argue.

“In the summer, living without electricity has been a matter of life or death,” said Jean Su, director of the Energy Justice Program at the Center for Biological Diversity. “We’ve seen the fatal consequences.”

Only half of states and the District of Columbia provide LIHEAP aid for summer utility bills. Last year, about 5 million people received help with heating costs, but only about 1 million households were assisted with cooling expenses, Wolfe said.

Mid Delta Community Services in Helena, Arkansas, has been fielding more and earlier calls than usual for its summer cooling program, said Sherrie Palmer, the nonprofit’s community programs director.

Just the requests to date could drain Mid Delta’s $678,000 allotment for cooling assistance.

“The need is great, especially when you have people who have to make a choice between eating and paying their utility bills,” Palmer said.

Zellie Word, who received help from Mid Delta earlier this year to pay her electric and gas bills, said she’s not sure how she’ll be able to afford air conditioning in coming months. She already had her electricity turned off for two weeks in April until she was able to borrow money to pay the tab.Luckily, she said, it was cool outdoors.

That’s not the case anymore. The temperatures in West Helena, where she lives, were forecasted to top 90 degrees several days this past week.

“It’s depressing,” said Word, 58, who works as a custodian at a local college. “I’m worried more than ever about maintaining my bills.”
